blocks.html: A data structure is a way of arranging data in memory so that it can be used efficiently. You already know one data structure: the array. In an array you can reach any element directly, for example marks[5] . Some problems, though, need data to be added and removed in a fixed order. For those we use special data structures such as the stack (this chapter) and the queue (Chapter 4).

blocks.html: A stack is a linear data structure in which items are added and removed only at one end, called the top. The item added last is the first one to be removed. This rule is called LIFO: Last In, First Out.

items.html: A stack of plates at a wedding buffet. Clean plates are placed on top, and guests take the top plate first.
Bangles on a wrist. The bangle worn last comes off first.
The Undo button (Ctrl+Z). The last change you made is undone first.
The Back button in a browser. It takes you to the page you visited most recently.
Books piled on a table. To reach the bottom book, you must first remove the ones above it.
The function call stack: when main() calls f1() and f1() calls f2() , they are stored on a stack. You saw this in Chapter 1 (stack unwinding).

blocks.html: Limitation: an array stack has a fixed size (MAX ). It can overflow even when the computer has plenty of memory left.
Each item is stored in a node that also holds a pointer to the node below it. The stack grows and shrinks as needed, so it never overflows (until the computer runs out of memory).
The C++ Standard Library gives a ready stack in the header <stack> . In real programs, use this one.

blocks.html: People write infix, but computers prefer postfix: it needs no brackets and no precedence rules, and a stack can calculate it in one left-to-right pass.

blocks.text: Operator precedence used in this chapter

items.html: Read the infix expression from left to right, one symbol at a time.
Operand (A, B, 5 ...): write it straight to the output.
( : push it.
) : pop and write operators until ( is found, then pop and discard the ( .
Operator: while the top of the stack is an operator of higher or equal precedence (for

blocks.html: ^ , only higher), pop it to the output. Then push the current operator.

items.html: At the end, pop all remaining operators to the output.

items.html: Read the postfix expression from left to right.
Number: push it.
Operator: pop two values. The first value popped is the right operand (B), and the second is the left operand (A). Calculate A op B and push the result.
At the end, the stack holds exactly one value: the answer.

items.html: A data structure organises data so that it can be used efficiently.
A stack is a linear data structure in which insertion and deletion happen only at one end, the top. It follows LIFO (Last In, First Out).
Main operations: push (add on top), pop (remove the top), peek/top (look at the top), isEmpty, isFull and size.
Overflow means pushing onto a full stack. Underflow means popping from an empty stack.
An array stack uses an index top (−1 when empty) and has a fixed size. A linked stack grows as needed. std::stack from <stack> is the ready-made version.
std::stack::pop() returns nothing. Use top() to read the item first, and check empty() before either.
Applications: reversing, undo/redo, the browser Back button, function calls, balanced brackets, and expression conversion and evaluation.
Postfix notation needs no brackets. Convert infix to postfix with an operator stack, and evaluate postfix with an operand stack.
In postfix evaluation, the first value popped is the right operand.
